answer.answer:
Deliver the panels through a kit-of-parts configurator sitting on a highly standardised component set: that is the route the record gives from prefabrication to mass-customisation, and it is what lets panels vary without the production line varying. Prefabrication itself has five requirements upstream of it, and not one of them is a machine: precise up-front planning, which 36 of the 50 coded cases draw on, then regulatory and certification compliance, early contractor involvement, DfMA for the fabrication process and an integrated supply chain, each drawn on by 12 to 15 cases. What you get back is schedule, quality, error reduction and site safety; what you must watch is that bespoke, customised design constrains modularity, and that design compromise through over-standardisation and production and assembly restriction are each coded in a sizeable share of the cases. Minergie, and energy certification generally, is absent from the record, so nothing here speaks to the envelope performance target itself.

**The route to non-repeating panels.** Two edges carry it. AT7 "Highly standardised" enablesCapability AR6 "Configurators/kit-of-parts" (DEP43, standard-grade evidence), on the ground that modular coordination permits the interchangeability of different components [1], and AR6 "Configurators/kit-of-parts" enablesCapability PR11 "Mass-customisation" (DEP75, peer-reviewed), the design configurator integrating customisation data into robotic manufacturing [1]. Read in direction: the standardised component grammar is upstream of the configurator, and the configurator is upstream of the varied output. The counts are uneven and the difference matters: 25 of the 50 coded cases draw on AT7 "Highly standardised" [1], 17 on PR11 "Mass-customisation" [1], but only 12 on AR6 "Configurators/kit-of-parts" [1]. The configurator is the scarce piece of the chain, not the standardisation.

The counterweight is DEP59, AT1 "Bespoke/customised design" constrains AT2 "Modular" (peer-reviewed): integral architecture couples functions tightly to components, constraining modular interchange [1]. 10 cases draw on AT1 "Bespoke/customised design" [1] against 12 on AT2 "Modular" [1]. If the non-repetition is geometric variation within a fixed interface set, the configurator route holds; if it is genuinely bespoke panel architecture, that edge says the modular logic degrades.

**What prefabrication requires.** PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site" carries 4 inbound and 6 outbound dependency edges, all listed in the context, and is drawn on by 20 of the 50 coded cases [1], so its requirement set can be quoted as complete. Two are its own dependsOn edges: PR2 dependsOn RI14 "Rely on precise planning", because prefabrication relies on precise up-front planning and logistics, peer-reviewed [2], and PR2 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern" (DEP96, peer-reviewed), a functional regulatory system for offsite compliance requiring third-party certification and traceability [1]. Three more feed it from upstream: CO11 "Early contractor involvement" enablesCapability PR2 (DEP22, peer-reviewed), since integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party to be involved in the early design phase [1]; PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process" enablesCapability PR2 (DEP15, peer-reviewed), DfMA orienting the project toward offsite manufacture [1]; and VA14 "Integrate supply chain" enablesCapability PR2 (DEP79, peer-reviewed), supply chain integration supporting the offsite production line [1]. The counts differ by roughly threefold across this set: 36 of 50 for RI14 "Rely on precise planning" [1], 15 for PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process" [1], 14 for VA14 "Integrate supply chain" [1], 14 for CO11 "Early contractor involvement" [1] and 12 for RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern" [1]. Planning discipline is close to universal; the contractual and supply-chain moves are the minority practice.

If the panels are robotically assembled rather than hand-laid in the factory, add DEP55: PR4 "Robotic assembly" hasPrecondition PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site", automated delivery and assembly requiring extensive prefabrication and unification of materials, peer-reviewed [1]. 13 of the 50 cases draw on PR4 "Robotic assembly" [1].

**What it returns.** All four outbound value edges from PR2 are peer-reviewed: VA2 "Reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency" (DEP17), offsite factory work compressing schedule [1], VA3 "Improve quality/performance" (DEP18), the controlled factory environment improving quality [1], VA13 "Improve site safety" (DEP19), moving work offsite improving site safety [1], and VA10 "Reduce errors/constraints" (DEP80), factory-based production improving quality control and reducing errors and rework [1]. VA13 "Improve site safety" carries 1 inbound and 0 outbound edges and is drawn on by 39 of 50 cases [1], so prefabrication is the only cited path into site safety in this material.

**Envelope performance and certification.** There is no Minergie node and no energy-certification enabler in the context. The nearest items are VA4 "Material/energy saving/reduce CO2/waste", drawn on by 15 of 50 c [1]
